items.title: Optimizing GPU Memory for Long Context
items.abstract:
Optimizing GPU Memory for Long Context was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on serving and optimizing large models under real production constraints. The project referenced by this session is Dao-AILab/flash-attention. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source flash-attention project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

A detailed section covers cache reuse, prefix sharing, and eviction policies, with guidance on when the complexity of a shared cache pays for itself.

A final segment maps model size and context length to realistic single-node and multi-node deployment envelopes.

The speaker highlights easy wins first: better batching, fewer copies, tighter tokenizers, and honest load tests before investing in exotic kernels.

Quantization is presented as a pipeline rather than a single switch: calibration, outlier handling, kernel support, and accuracy regression checks all matter.

The speaker frames serving as a scheduling problem: requests, KV cache blocks, batching windows, and hardware memory all compete for the same resources.

Continuous batching and paged attention are explained through production traces rather than benchmark charts, including the tail latency effects that appear when long and short requests mix.

Method and measurement. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed.

Takeaways. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement. The main takeaway is to measure the bottleneck before redesigning the architecture. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check.

Session context. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. The room was full, and the questions after the talk focused on deployment details rather than demos. The speaker contrasted research prototypes with systems that must run unattended overnight and recover from partial failures.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

items.title: An Open Bibliography for Agent Research
items.abstract:
An Open Bibliography for Agent Research was recorded as a Panel session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on the engineering of reliable agents, tool use, orchestration, and state management. The project referenced by this session is srush/awesome-o1. Programme notes describe the project as: An open bibliography and survey that curates papers, notes, and slide sources on reasoning and test-time compute for LLM agents. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Human-in-the-loop controls are treated as a first-class feature rather than an afterthought: approval gates, diff previews, and escalation policies are designed before the agent is deployed.

Several examples show how to keep an agent grounded in an environment: sandboxed file systems, browser sessions, shell access, and structured observations that the model can verify.

The team presents a checklist for reliability: deterministic tool adapters, idempotent actions, checkpointed state, and replayable transcripts for every long-running task.

The talk closes with cost and latency accounting, showing where orchestration overhead dominates and how caching, batching, and concurrency limits change the economics of agent products.

The speaker opens with a taxonomy of agent runtimes: planners, executors, tool routers, memory services, and policy layers that decide when an autonomous loop should stop and ask for help.

The session compares single-agent loops with multi-agent topologies and argues that most production failures come from unclear handoffs rather than weak models.

Method and measurement. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces. The speaker explains how they decided which optimizations were worth maintaining and which were removed after the experiment. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed.

Takeaways. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question.
